content: Mifepristone is a medication that can interact with other drugs by influencing the metabolism of the hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. This interaction can either increase or decrease the levels and effects of certain medications, necessitating careful monitoring or adjustments in therapy. For example: 1. Vinorelbine: Mifepristone may alter its metabolism via CYP3A4, requiring caution and close monitoring. 2. Voclosporin: Mifepristone increases its levels or effects through CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitoring is essential. 3. Vorapaxar: Mifepristone raises its levels or effects via CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 4. Voriconazole: This drug increases mifepristone levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification and close monitoring are necessary. Do not exceed 300 mg/day of mifepristone for Cushing’s syndrome when combined with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, as this combination may also prolong the QT interval. 5. Vorinostat: Mifepristone may increase QT interval effects. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. 6. Vortioxetine: Mifepristone increases its levels or effects via CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 7. Warfarin: Mifepristone enhances its anticoagulant effects, making this combination contraindicated. 8. Zanubrutinib: Mifepristone increases its levels or effects via CYP3A4 metabolism. Reduce zanubrutinib to 80 mg daily when co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Resume the previous dose after discontinuing the inhibitor. 9. Ziprasidone: Mifepristone may increase QT interval effects. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 10. Zolpidem: Mifepristone increases its levels or effects via CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 11. Zuranolone: Mifepristone decreases its levels or effects via CYP3A4 metabolism. Dose reduction of zuranolone may be necessary when combined with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Common Side Effects: Mifepristone is associated with several side effects, including: Gastrointestinal: Abdominal pain (96%), uterine cramping (83%), nausea (43-61%), vomiting (1-26%), diarrhea (12-20%). Neurological: Headache (2-44%), dizziness (1-12%), fatigue (48%), somnolence (10%). Endocrine/Metabolic: Hypokalemia (34%), decreased appetite (20%), abnormal thyroid function tests (18%), hypoglycemia (5-10%). Musculoskeletal: Arthralgia (30%), myalgia (14%), back pain (9-16%), extremity pain (12%). Cardiovascular: Hypertension (24%), peripheral edema (26%). Other: Endometrial hypertrophy (38%), vaginal bleeding or metrorrhagia (5-10%), rash (4%), pruritus (4%), sinusitis (2-14%), nasopharyngitis (12%), viral infections (4%). Contraindications: Mifepristone is contraindicated in pregnancy as it causes pregnancy loss. Women of childbearing age must confirm they are not pregnant before starting treatment and use reliable non-hormonal contraception during and for one month after stopping the medication. It is also contraindicated in individuals with known hypersensitivity to mifepristone, misoprostol, or other prostaglandins. Breastfeeding: Mifepristone is present in human milk, but the amount and effects on breastfed infants or milk production are unknown. Mechanism of Action: Mifepristone is an antiprogestin that stimulates uterine contractility and increases prostaglandin levels by inhibiting prostaglandin dehydrogenase. It also blocks cortisol receptor binding, reducing the effects of excess cortisol, such as hyperglycemia, in conditions like Cushing’s syndrome. Pharmacokinetics: Peak Plasma Time: 1-2 hours (single dose), 1-4 hours (multiple doses). Protein Binding: >99% to alpha-1-acid glycoprotein. Metabolism: Extensively metabolized by CYP3A4 into three active metabolites. Half-life: 20 hours (single dose), 85 hours (multiple doses). Excretion: 90% via feces. Administration: Take mifepristone orally with a meal, as directed by your doctor, usually once daily. Swallow tablets whole without splitting, crushing, or chewing. Avoid grapefruit or grapefruit juice during treatment, as it may increase side effects. Monitoring: Follow up with your healthcare provider 7-14 days after taking Mifeprex. Storage: Store at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Properly discard expired or unused medication. Important Warnings: Mifepristone may cause QT prolongation, a condition affecting heart rhythm. Risk factors include low potassium or magnesium levels, certain medications, and medical conditions like severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. This medication may decrease the effectiveness of hormonal birth control methods, increasing the risk of pregnancy. Discuss alternative non-hormonal contraception with your doctor. Overdose: In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention. In the U.S., call 911 or the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about mifepristone. Always consult your healthcare provider for personalized advice and complete information about this medication.
